chapter_theme: The Chola queen, grieving her son, has Manimekalai released into her keeping and tries to destroy her by drug, slander and starvation; each trick fails by the knowledge and mantras Manimekalai has gained, and when the queen repents Manimekalai teaches her that grief for a body is idle, that the prince died by his own past deed, and that lust, killing, drink, falsehood and theft must be renounced, until the queen's grief is quenched and the two bow to each other.

cast.role: an old woman of the Chola court whose counsel soothes king, prince and queen
the Chola queen, Udayakumaran's mother, who plots against Manimekalai and is taught by her
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
Madhavi's daughter, the Buddhist ascetic held in the palace
an unlettered youth the queen hires to dishonour Manimekalai

manimekalai:23:1-16.reading: By the king's leave the old woman Vasanthavai, whose counsel soothes king, prince and queen alike, goes to the grieving queen Rajamadevi, bows to her without weeping at her feet, and reminds her that in this conquering line even a king who dies old is laid on darbha grass and cut with a sword so that he may go where battle-loving kings go, since a quiet death is a shame to the house.
manimekalai:23:1-16.nuance: Her consolation is a rebuke: she does not weep with the queen (9, அழுது அடி வீழாது) and offers the warrior code's rite for a non-heroic death, the rite Purananuru 93 describes, as the measure by which the prince's death is to be judged.
manimekalai:23:1-16.event: Vasanthavai goes to the grieving queen, bows, and tells her of the rite by which kings of this line who die old are cut with a sword on darbha grass.

claims.claim: for those born in the royal line, to die of old age without a wound is a shame

manimekalai:23:17-40.reading: Vasanthavai ends by asking what the prince's death can be called, since he died neither guarding his own land nor taking another's, and bids the queen not grieve before the king; the queen hides her grief, resolves to deceive Manimekalai, and tells the king that the prince had lost his wits and his kingly conduct while the girl who has risen to wisdom does not deserve prison, so the king lets her take Manimekalai into her palace, where the queen privately vows to turn the girl's mind and make her a spectacle for the city.
manimekalai:23:17-40.nuance: The queen's plea for release is true in content and false in aim: the narrator frames it with her hidden grief and false conduct (21 to 23) and her private vow (39 to 40). Lines 31 to 34 quote a saying on whom kings should honour and whom set aside, and who speaks 31 to 36 is not plain: the queen may continue to 34 and the king answer at 35 to 36, or the king may speak from 31. The words கையாற்று and பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம் (21 to 22) return in Manimekalai's teaching at 124 to 125.
manimekalai:23:17-40.event: The queen, concealing her grief and intent, persuades the king to release Manimekalai from prison into her keeping and takes her into the palace.

claims.claim: a prince's death is honourable only when he dies guarding his own land or seizing another's
imprisonment does not befit one who has turned to wisdom and given up youth's pleasures

manimekalai:23:41-56.reading: The queen feeds Manimekalai a drug meant to derange her, but having known her former birth she stays clear-minded; the queen then pays an unlettered youth a handful of coins to go to her, make marks of lovemaking on her body and tell everyone she has lain with him, and when he comes to her room Manimekalai, seeing the queen's trick, chants her mantra and sits in a man's form, so that the youth, finding a man in the royal women's quarters, flees in fear, calling the queen a woman fit for hell.
manimekalai:23:41-56.nuance: The trick aims at the one thing an ascetic woman's standing rests on, report (46 to 47, பலர்க்கு உரை); the mantra of changing form given her in kaathai 10 answers it, and the hired youth, not the narrator, is the first to name the queen's cruelty (56).
manimekalai:23:41-56.event: The queen drugs Manimekalai and hires a youth to dishonour her; Manimekalai stays clear-minded and takes a man's form by a mantra, and the youth flees.

claims.claim: one who has come to know her former birth is not deluded

manimekalai:23:57-71.reading: Asking why she should keep the one who brought ruin on her son, the queen gives out that Manimekalai has stopped eating from an incurable illness and shuts her in a stifling cell, but the mantra that does away with food keeps her unharmed; the queen trembles, bows and begs forgiveness for wronging an ascetic out of grief for her son, and Manimekalai begins her answer by asking where the queen was weeping on the day the serpent with fiery eyes took the life of Rahulan, son of Neelapathi, and she herself, unable to bear it, burned her own life.
manimekalai:23:57-71.nuance: The false illness (59, ஊண் ஒழிந்தனள்) is made literally true by the mantra (61, ஊண் ஒழி மந்திரம்) without harm, so the lie defeats itself. Manimekalai's question turns on the same life having died before: the queen did not weep for Rahulan, and weeps now for Udayakumaran, who is that Rahulan reborn.
manimekalai:23:57-71.event: The queen starves Manimekalai in a closed cell under a pretended illness; the mantra keeps her well, and the queen repents and begs her forgiveness.

manimekalai:23:72-85.reading: Manimekalai tells the queen she has done what is unfitting and asks whether she weeps for the body or the life: if for the body, who but the mourners cast her son into the burning ground, and if for the life, where it enters next is set by its deeds and hard to know, so that one who loves that life should pity every life; and she tells her that the thief who killed her son was his own violent deed, the cutting down of a cook who fell and broke the serving vessels, which rose in wrath, took his life once by a serpent and ended it now by the vidyadhara's sword.
manimekalai:23:72-85.nuance: The 'thief' (கள்வன், 81) who killed the prince is the deed itself, not Kanchanan, whose sword is only its instrument (85); the deed is said to 'rise in wrath' (83, உருத்து எழும்), the verb of the Silappathikaram's moral of karma. Manimekalai speaks of a life (உயிர்) entering a dwelling (புக்கில், 76) by its deeds; the text puts the Buddhist teaching in these words without raising the question of a lasting self.
manimekalai:23:72-85.event: Manimekalai answers the queen's grief and tells her that the prince's death was the fruit of his killing of a cook in a former birth.

claims.claim: grief for the body is idle, since the mourners themselves carry it to the burning ground
where a life goes after death is fixed by its own deeds and is hard to know
one who loves a single life must show pity to every life
a violent deed of a former birth rises again and takes the doer's life, here twice, by serpent and by sword

manimekalai:23:86-97.reading: Saying that if the queen asks how she knows this she will tell, Manimekalai recounts everything from entering the flowering grove to grasping the deity's words, and then says that because the queen's drug found her already knowing her former birth she was not deluded, that when the unlettered lout came in the dark she held a man's form, and that it was her mantra against hunger that made the queen's deceit fail.
manimekalai:23:86-97.nuance: Lines 92 to 94 repeat lines 41 to 43 almost word for word, with the narrator's third person turned into her first: she tells the queen her own plot, so that the confession the queen made in 64 to 66 is met with full knowledge, not with discovery.
manimekalai:23:86-97.event: Manimekalai tells the queen her story from the grove onward and how each of the queen's tricks failed.

manimekalai:23:98-112.reading: Manimekalai says she did not set her mind on flying off or changing her form to escape, but stayed so as to remove the grief of the queen who bore her beloved of the former birth and to end her evil deed, and bids her hear sweet words: in a land thrown into turmoil by its rulers, a weaver's wife abandoned by her husband and parted from her infant went off and lived as a woman without bounds, and the son, raised by a brahmin without the townsfolk knowing whose he was, lay with her unknowing and, learning the truth, gave up his life.
manimekalai:23:98-112.nuance: The stories that follow (104 to 123) answer, one by one, to unchaste desire, killing, drink, falsehood and theft, which 126 to 129 gather as 'these' to be renounced; the text does not name the set. Whether 98 to 99 means she refrained from using her powers against the queen, or that she lacked them in her former birth, turns on where 'சென்ற பிறவியில்' attaches; காருக மடந்தை is read as a weaver's wife.
manimekalai:23:98-112.event: Manimekalai tells the queen of a son who unknowingly lay with his abandoned mother and gave up his life on learning it.

manimekalai:23:113-130.reading: She goes on: a forest hunter shot a doe big with young so that the fawn fell from her torn belly, and seeing the tears in her red eye he gave up his life; drunkards who go before a rutting elephant are gored on its white tusk, such is the pride of toddy; those who take the way of falsehood as their gain never pass beyond helpless grief; and the queen should not tell herself that such sufferings belong to thieves alone, for to all who live in this great world these bring sorrow and must be renounced, and learning that is merely learned is not learning.
manimekalai:23:113-130.nuance: 124 to 125 turn on the queen the very words the narrator used of her at 21 to 22 (கையாற்று, பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம்): the general lesson is aimed at her own conduct. Line 130 runs into the next unit's definition of true learning.
manimekalai:23:113-130.event: Manimekalai tells of a hunter who died of remorse at a dying doe's tears and of drunkards gored by an elephant, and urges the queen to renounce such ways.

claims.claim: those who take falsehood as their way of gain never escape helpless grief
the sufferings that follow these deeds are not for thieves alone; all who live in the world must renounce them

manimekalai:23:131-147.reading: Manimekalai ends that the truly learned are those who have curbed hatred and understood fully, who supply what the suffering lack, who know the world to come, who end the hunger of those who come wearied, who grasp the firm truth that cuts off sorrow, and whose love for all creatures never ceases; so she pours the clear water of wisdom into the queen's ear and quenches the fire of grief that had her mind for fuel, and the queen, cleared like water settled by the clearing-nut and no longer hostile, bows to her, but Manimekalai cannot bear it, bows and praises her in return, saying she has done what is not fitting, for she is the mother of her beloved and the king's great queen.
manimekalai:23:131-147.nuance: The queen's bow (144) would set the ascetic above the queen; Manimekalai's returned bow (147) restores the order of kinship from her former birth, so the reconciliation is completed in family terms as well as doctrinal ones. The grief-as-fire image (140 to 141) and the clearing-nut image (142) make the teaching a medicine rather than a refutation.
manimekalai:23:131-147.event: The queen's grief is quenched by Manimekalai's teaching; she bows to Manimekalai, who bows to her in return.

claims.claim: true learning is curbing hatred, relieving the hunger and want of others, grasping the truth that ends sorrow and keeping love for all creatures

links.note: Both give the rite of laying a king who died of sickness on darbha grass and cutting him with a sword with the words 'go where the warriors go' (செல்வுழிச் செல்க in both); Avvai uses it to praise Athiyaman's battle wounds, Vasanthavai to console and rebuke a queen whose son died in neither war nor old age.
links.teaches: Held together they show the rite outliving its Sangam use as praise: in the epic it becomes the standard by which a dead prince is found wanting, so that the warrior code is used to stop a mother's grief rather than to honour a king.

gains.a: the Sangam source of the custom, which shows that Vasanthavai is quoting an old royal code of the warrior's death and not inventing a comfort
gains.b: a later witness that the rite was remembered as a royal custom and could be turned from praise of the wounded against a prince who died without honour

links.note: The Manimekala goddess gave Manimekalai mantras to take another form, travel the sky and end hunger, warning that people would not tell a young woman the truth; here the form-changing mantra defeats the queen's plot.
links.teaches: The pair shows why the goddess's gifts were defensive: the mantra of another form, given against those who would not trust a young woman, is first used to save her from a slander about her body.

links.note: The sage foretold that Rahulan would die of the serpent's venomous gaze within sixteen days and that Lakshmi would burn with him; Manimekalai now uses that death to ask the queen why she did not weep for the same life then.
links.teaches: The prophecy of a death in the former birth becomes, in this kaathai, the ground of an argument against grief: the same life has died before unmourned by its present mother, so her grief is for this body only.

links.note: Tirumular describes the whole town wailing, renaming the dead man a corpse, burning him and bathing to forget; Manimekalai asks the queen whether she weeps for the body, since mourners themselves cast it into the burning ground, or for the life, whose next dwelling is set by deeds.
links.teaches: Tirumular's observation that mourners burn and forget the body they weep for becomes in the epic the first horn of a dilemma whose second horn turns grief for one life into pity for all lives.

gains.a: a plain picture of the mourners' contradiction that her terse question 'who cast him into the burning ground?' assumes
gains.b: a use for the observation: the Buddhist teacher draws from it an obligation of compassion, not only the impermanence the verse leaves the reader with

links.note: The Silappathikaram's patikam sets as a moral that the deed of the past comes in wrath and feeds its fruit (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Manimekalai uses the same verb of the prince's former killing of a cook (உருத்து எழும் வல் வினை).
links.teaches: The pair shows the sequel taking its companion's moral from the frame into a mechanism: here the wrathful deed is named, traced across two births and two deaths, and offered to a mourner as consolation rather than as a verdict on a king.

links.note: The pillar deity told Manimekalai that the prince's death came from his killing of the cook who broke the vessels meant for the sage Brahmadharma; Manimekalai now passes that revelation to the prince's mother.
links.teaches: The same account of a past killing changes use between the two kaathais: revealed to the lover as the reason for his death, it is retold to the mother as the reason not to hate the woman she blamed for it.

links.note: Kural 284 says that a love grown in stealth yields at harvest a sorrow that does not die; Manimekalai tells the queen not to think that the harsh suffering of those who live by stealth is for thieves alone, since these ways bring sorrow to all who live in the world.
links.teaches: The couplet assigns undying sorrow to the thief; the epic refuses to let a listener file that sorrow under a class of criminals and extends it to a queen whose fault was deceit, making the rule about theft a rule about all concealment.

gains.a: a known rule on the fruit of stealth, which gives force to the phrase she will not let the queen keep at a distance
gains.b: a scene in which the couplet's reader is warned against using it to sort the guilty from herself

links.note: The narrator says the queen hid her grief with helpless heart (கையாற்று) and false conduct (பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம்); Manimekalai's maxim says those who take falsehood as their way never pass beyond helpless grief (பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம், கையாற்று அவலம்).
links.teaches: Read together, the maxim is not general advice but the queen's own conduct described back to her in the narrator's words, so the teaching names her deceit without accusing her.

links.note: Kural 2 asks what learning is worth if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Manimekalai says learning that is merely learned is not learning, and names the learned as those who curb hatred, end hunger and love all creatures.
links.teaches: Both refuse learning its own worth, but the couplet completes it in worship while the epic completes it in compassion and the ending of others' hunger, so the pair shows two answers to the same question of what learning is for.

gains.a: a classic statement that learning needs a further end, against which her list reads as a choice of ends
gains.b: a Buddhist answer to its question that puts the further end in conduct toward beings rather than in reverence to a lord

links.note: Gotami, mourning her son at the burning ground, begged the goddess to take her life for his and was told a life gone goes by its deeds; the queen, mourning her son, is taught the same and her grief is quenched.
links.teaches: The epic answers a mother's grief twice with the same doctrine but to opposite ends: Gotami, refused, dies beside her son, while the queen, taught to turn her love to all lives, is cleared and bows to her son's supposed enemy.

source_issues: Line 140 carries the kaathai number 223 in its line mark; read as 23-140 (flagged by show).
Lines 51, 89, 138 and 142 had ௌ for ெள, repaired in the core (flagged by show).
Lines 31 to 36: the saying in 31 to 32 is hard to construe, and the change of speaker between the queen and the king (34, இறை சொல; 35 to 36) is not marked.
Lines 98 to 100: whether சென்ற பிறவியில் belongs with 'I did not set my mind on' or with காதலற் பயந்தோய் is unclear; and காருக மடந்தை (105) is a rare expression.
